input: An urgent-care note from last winter records Persistent BP 178/104 mmHg before treatment, while today's seated BP 146/88 mmHg was taken once and a pharmacy receipt from three days earlier shows 154/92 without documenting the rest period or cuff size.
One event followed a long period without food, another occurred after breakfast, and there is no witness account detailed enough to establish whether either episode involved loss of consciousness.
The nurse records unresolved symptoms and inconsistent timing rather than a confirmed medication adverse effect, persistent current pressure or a diagnosed cause of collapse.

During review the driver describes increased thirst, frequent overnight urination and fluctuating blur over approximately three weeks, but says a diagnosis of diabetes has never been confirmed for him; his sister uses insulin, and he is concerned that this means he must have the same condition.

He brought an optometry card from eight months ago recording corrected right eye 6/6 and left eye 6/9, yet says the current blur varies during the day and is sometimes accompanied by glare rather than two separate images.
He denies a persistent double image, has not had a current visual field examination and cannot determine whether the symptoms change when either eye is covered.
The referral mentions possible diabetes and requests further assessment, but it does not document a confirmed diagnosis, diabetic eye disease or a treatment plan.

His older occupational form states vision was satisfactory at that time; the nurse has not treated that statement as proof of present visual fitness or attributed the new symptoms to a particular metabolic cause.
